strengths: Addresses an important evaluation problem: whether proliferating benchmarks measure distinct capabilities, and whether performance correlations obscure meaningful differences.

Using predictive token perplexities as benchmark signatures is an interesting extension of prior corpus-selection methods. The distinction between semantic, performance, and signature overlap provides a useful framework for investigation.

The study includes substantial empirical work across 32 models and 88 benchmark/subtask outputs, with public data, model identifiers, and algorithm descriptions. The reported leave-one-out MAE improvement from 0.180 to 0.075 provides preliminary evidence of predictive signal.
weaknesses: The feature-selection regime raises severe overfitting concerns. Appendix E.1 describes 16.9 million candidate features, approximately 338,000 retained after screening, and typically 30 selected predictors for only 32 observations. Ordinary AIC does not adequately address this enormous adaptive search. Section 3.2 does not establish that both screening and forward selection are repeated inside each cross-validation fold; otherwise, held-out labels influence feature selection. Fully nested validation, held-out model families, permutation controls, and selection-stability measurements are needed.

Predictive regression does not establish the validity of the proposed overlap measure. Sections 3.3 and E.1 discard fitted coefficients and instead correlate unweighted averages of normalized perplexities, despite selecting features from both positive and negative correlation tails. Predictive validity therefore does not automatically transfer to this aggregation. More dispersed heatmaps and intuitive examples do not demonstrate that signatures recover shared capabilities; external validation and concrete signature examples are missing.

The claim that signatures resolve benchmark-family and question-format bias is unsupported. Near-zero correlations can reflect lost signal, and nonsignificant differences in Figure 5 do not establish equivalence or invariance. Benchmark-pair correlations share benchmarks and models, violating the independence assumed by an ordinary Mann–Whitney comparison. Family and format are also entangled in the reported comparisons. Controlled reformattings of the same questions and dependence-aware uncertainty estimates are necessary before attributing these patterns to format or claiming its effects are removed.

The semantic baseline is materially weakened by its implementation. Algorithm 3 concatenates benchmark questions and truncates the result to the encoder's maximum length, repeatedly retaining the same prefix of the smaller benchmark. Consequently, most questions may never contribute. Item-level embeddings with appropriate aggregation would provide a more credible comparison. The evaluation also lacks performance correlations adjusted for overall model ability and predictive baselines using average corpus loss or model size.

Cross-model token perplexities are not clearly comparable. The method scores the last tokenizer token of each whitespace-delimited target across models with different tokenizers, potentially comparing different subword events. Within-model z-scoring does not resolve this target mismatch. The reference population used for z-scoring is also unspecified. A common textual scoring unit and tokenizer-sensitivity analysis are important for interpreting the resulting signatures.

The sparsity and granularity arguments exceed their evidence. A correlation distribution concentrated near zero with extreme tails can arise under a null model, especially when millions of features are searched. Appendix C does not establish the conditions needed to transfer SIS guarantees to this procedure. Likewise, Table 1 measures dispersion of correlations rather than held-out predictive accuracy or reliability of benchmark relationships, so it does not establish the claimed superiority of token-level signatures.

Reproducibility and the breadth of conclusions remain limited. No code, extracted signatures, full performance matrix, or per-benchmark validation results are supplied, and prompting, few-shot, and decoding settings are insufficiently specified. Appendix E.1's corpus counts are inconsistent: dividing 8.45 billion by 50 does not yield 16.9 million. Most evaluated tasks come from MMLU and BBH, with limited independent coding coverage and no clearly identified multilingual suite, weakening broad conclusions about coding distinctiveness, multilingual capabilities, and the general LLM capability landscape.

Feature selection presents a substantial overfitting risk: approximately 30 predictors are selected for only 32 model observations after searching millions of candidates (A.5.1). AIC does not adequately address this enormous adaptive search. The LOOCV description does not establish whether screening and selection are repeated entirely within each fold. The two held-out models are useful evidence, but family-disjoint validation, permutation controls, and validation of the overlap matrix itself remain missing. Bell-shaped correlation distributions also do not establish the claimed sparse signal structure.

The comparisons do not convincingly establish superiority. Algorithm 3 concatenates benchmark questions and truncates them to the embedding model's maximum length, leaving the smaller benchmark represented by a fixed initial fragment. This makes the semantic baseline incomplete and order-sensitive. Performance comparisons also omit stronger alternatives such as general-ability-adjusted correlations and latent-factor models. Greater heatmap contrast alone is not evidence of more accurate capability measurement.

The claim that evaluation bias is resolved is stronger than the evidence (Section 4.2). Nonsignificant within-versus-between differences do not establish invariance to format or benchmark family, and regression on confounded performance labels does not automatically remove those confounds. Matched-content format interventions are absent. Moreover, benchmark-pair correlations share models and benchmarks; the statistical procedures do not clearly account for these dependencies or uncertainty introduced by feature selection.

Cross-model token comparability is insufficiently addressed. Recording the last model token of a whitespace-delimited piece can score different substrings under different tokenizers (A.2 and A.5.1). Within-model z-scoring does not ensure that these are comparable prediction events. Tokenization could therefore contribute to apparent capability structure; a common-string likelihood or comparable normalization ablation is needed.

Several interpretations exceed the study's coverage. Coding is represented by MBPP, which is insufficient to establish that coding broadly constitutes an isolated or comparatively 'clean' capability. Likewise, semantic mismatch between selected snippets and task labels does not establish differences between LLM semantic organization and human conceptual structure. These findings should remain exploratory hypotheses.

Reproducibility has material gaps and inconsistencies. A.5.1 states that downsampling 8.45 billion instances by 1/50 yields 16.9 million, whereas it yields 169 million; the relationship to the stated 1B-token corpus is also unclear. The reference population for z-scoring and exact evaluation configurations need specification. The abstract's code-release sentence is unfinished and supplies no repository link. These issues, together with the unresolved validity and evaluation concerns, leave the contribution below the acceptance threshold.
